messages.body_plain:
late reply, sorry

>
> (1 ) Rhipe uses the Hadoop streaming facility to run the map reduce
> jobs. It encapsulates the map and reduce expression along with the
> other Hadoop related parameters and then it uses the Hadoop Streaming
> facility to submit the jobs.
>
> (2) The map and reduce programs runs on the R environment.
>
> Now the mapper and reducer  tasks has to run on the JVM,
> Q1) So how JVM runs the map and reduce function on the R environment?

Starts  R in the subprocess and feeds data via standard input and
reads from standard output and standard error
Other options a) use a local tcp/ip port but i think on linux, writing
and reading from standard * is very fast
or b) embed R using JNI - not sure if there any benefit here. There is
a rough cut on Github which doesn't
give correct results for combiners. Not sure if there is any
performance improvement (and whether it's worth all the JNI hassle)

>
> Q2) What  is happening internally? How does the sorting and shuffling
> is taking place?

Hadoop does sorting and shuffling. Default ordering is byte ordering
but you can sort on numeric values and string values
(even with vectors so that shorter vectors come before longer ones)
and partition on slices of the vector (if it is a
string/numeric/integer vector)

>
> A more general question is that why the Rhipe needs to installed on
> all the nodes? Since anyways the Rhipe submits the job to the Hadoop
> and its the hadoop MapReduce framework that parallelize the
> application, so is it not sufficient to install the Rhipe only on the
> namenode of the hadoop as the PIG does?
>

It can be done...see rhoptions()$runner, so one approach would be to

x <- rhoptions()$runner[1]
rhput(x,"/tmp/") # copy tp the DFS
rhoptions()$runner[1] = "./imperious.so"
rhmr(...., shared.files= c("/tmp/imperious.so")....)

It is crucial all the directories and paths are identical across
nodes. This /might/ work - try it out.
Don't have a cluster at hand right now to confirm.

Cheers
Saptarshi

I'd say we've made much progress! Your postscripts have answered your questions.
RHIPE in some sense is subtly typed, that is keys are compared in
Hadoop based on
comparing the byte representation. So integers are numerics are
different

> rhsz(1)
 [1] 08 02 12 08 00 00 00 00 00 00 f0 3f
> rhsz(1L)

Now, RHIPE is not doing any casting behind the scenes. In the line

X <- rhwrite(lapply(1:4, function(i) list(from=i,to=i+1)), A, 1)

rhwrite will check if the list has a names attribute
- if yes, that becomes reduce.keys
- if not, as.character(1:length(list)) becomes the keys
and if each element of the list is is list(a,b) it leaves it untouched
and write thes elements (like what you'd get from rhread) and this is
the case for X.

Anyway, in X, X[[1]][[1]] is an integer and X[[1]][[2]] is a numeric.
The X[[1]][[1]] is the
map.key and X[[1]][[2]] is the map.value.

Hope it helps

Saptarshi

information out of a map-reduce job  was working and I finally figured
out why.

In the context of using my experimental map/reduce as environments
system (since the original posting it has been modified but the jist
of which is posted here), I was getting an error at the time of the
map environment attach before the map functions got called.  Hence,
every strategy I used to get information out of the system inside the
map functions failed because the code never got called.

BTW if your wondering how an attach can make an error, it was because
I was trying to pass a subset argument and the subset needs to be
evaluated in the environment of data.frames in the map.keys.   I got a
plan for that though.

Since I realized that, I can now get the info I need.

Thanks,

I gave up on the logging when I figured out how to get my dump error
scheme to work again (I struggled with permissions on the cluster
until I thought it through clearly).  First thing I do now in setup
prior to any possible error is use:

errorFunc =  function() {
	local = ""
	try({if(!is.null(map.values)) local = "map."},silent=TRUE)
	try({if(!is.null(reduce.values)) local = "reduce."},silent=TRUE)
	uniqueid = paste(sample(letters,10,replace=TRUE),sep="",collapse="")
	filename = paste("error.env.",local, uniqueid,".RData",sep="")
	save.image(filename)
	errdir = "/wsc/tmp/jrounds/error/"
	#need to make the directory ahead of time and set permissions for
hadoop user to write.
	system(paste("hadoop dfs -put", filename, errdir))
	fullname = paste(errdir,filename,sep="")
	system(paste("hadoop dfs -chown jrounds", fullname))
}
options(error = errorFunc)

After an error occurs errdir has one Rdata file per a simultaneously
running job (tested on a cluster).

That seems to work quite well on the cluster.  Makes a directory of
error environments for inspection if there is an error.  I previously
mentioned it.  I just hadn't got around to getting the idea to work on
the cluster yet.  The only reason I mentioned on this thread is that
it is a personal narrative and explains why I abandoned any concept of
a log.  Though I guess the corollary to the question "how do you log
in a distributed environment?" has the answer: one log per a process
in a log directory.  That is really what I have with the saved
environments. One environment per a process given it created an
error.  Up to the user to inspect them for bugs.
